questions.q: A pod starts, crashes, and Kubernetes keeps restarting it, waiting longer each time. What status is that?
options: Pending, with a FailedScheduling event
ImagePullBackOff
CrashLoopBackOff, restarting
questions.why: The app starts, crashes, Kubernetes waits a little and starts it again. Back off means waiting longer between restarts; the app itself keeps crashing.
explanations: Pending, with a FailedScheduling event, means no node can take the pod yet: it never starts, so it can't crash.
ImagePullBackOff means the image can't be pulled, for example a typo in the tag: the container never starts.
Correct. In the lab, the worker that can't reach its database flips between Error and CrashLoopBackOff.
questions.takeaway: CrashLoopBackOff: the app runs and crashes. ImagePullBackOff: it never gets its image. Pending: no room to run.

questions.q: In one run, a single broken pod has written several Warning events, so four items reach this node. What does it pass on?
options: All four items, one per Warning event
One item for each broken pod's name
Only pods not seen in earlier runs
Only the newest event in the namespace
questions.why: One alert per pod removes duplicates inside this run by comparing the pod's name (involvedObject.name): several warnings from one pod become one item.
explanations: That would mean one alert per event: one broken pod would send several messages in the same run.
Correct. Four items became three: one per broken pod.
That is the next node, New problems only, which remembers earlier executions.
It keeps one item per pod, not one item for the whole namespace.
questions.takeaway: De-duplication step one: one item per pod within a run.

questions.q: A worker keeps crashing for an hour. The workflow checks every 30 seconds. How many alerts does the team get for that pod?
options: About 120
Exactly one alert
None at all
One every two minutes
questions.why: New problems only (Remove Duplicates, remove items processed in previous executions) remembers the pod names it already alerted on: one problem, one message.
explanations: That would be one alert per check: exactly the flood the workflow is built to avoid.
Correct. In the lesson, later executions passed nothing on: Format and Post didn't run.
The first check after the crash does alert: the pod is new to New problems only.
The two-minute window decides which events count as recent; it does not repeat alerts.
questions.takeaway: Remember what you already alerted on, or people stop trusting the channel.

questions.q: This Role is bound to n8n's ServiceAccount. What can n8n do with its token?
questions.code:
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: n8n-reader
  namespace: demo
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods", "events"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - apiGroups: ["apps"]
    resources: ["deployments"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
options: Read pods, events and deployments in demo only
Read pods, events and deployments in every namespace
Read and restart pods and deployments in demo
Read secrets in demo, as part of the core group
questions.why: The verbs are get, list and watch only; the resources are pods, events and deployments; and a Role, unlike a ClusterRole, only works inside its own namespace.
explanations: Correct. No create, no delete, no secrets, no other namespace.
A Role is namespaced: it only works inside demo. Every namespace would need a ClusterRole.
Restarting a pod means deleting or changing it, and no such verb is listed.
Secrets are not in the resources list, so they stay locked even though they are in the core group.
questions.takeaway: Least privilege: only the verbs, resources and namespace the workflow needs.

questions.q: The Get warning events node sends this request. What does it ask Kubernetes for?
options: Every event in the cluster
The pods in the namespace that aren't Running
A stream of new events pushed as they happen
The namespace's Warning events
questions.why: The URL is an expression: the cluster address from .env, then the events of our namespace, with a field selector type=Warning. The Authorization header uses the token from .env, which n8n never shows.
explanations: The path names one namespace, and the field selector keeps only Warning events.
This is the events endpoint. Pods are read by the second workflow, the daily health report.
This is polling: one request every 30 seconds. Push would need a watcher inside the cluster.
Correct. One item comes back, a list of events, which One item per event then splits.
questions.takeaway: Let the API filter for you (fieldSelector), and keep address and token in .env.

questions.q: You roll out a new web version with a typo in the image tag. kubectl rollout status times out. What are your users getting meanwhile?
options: Errors: Kubernetes removed the old pods first
Nothing: the deployment is scaled to zero pods
A mix of both versions
The old version, still running
questions.why: The rollout is stuck because the new pod can't pull its image (ImagePullBackOff), and the old pods keep serving. Kubernetes never removes the last good version for a broken one.
explanations: The old pods are replaced only when new ones are ready; the new one never becomes ready.
The deployment still asks for two copies, and the two old ones stay up.
The broken pod never starts, so it can't serve anyone.
Correct. Stuck rollout, old pods still serving; fix.sh rolls web back to the last good version.
questions.takeaway: A stuck rollout is bad news, not an outage: alert on it before someone rolls out again.

questions.q: A report pod stays Pending. kubectl describe shows: FailedScheduling, 0/1 nodes are available: insufficient CPU. What is the cause?
options: It asks for more CPU than any node has free
The image tag in the new version has a typo
The app crashes at start-up and backs off
n8n's token can't read the demo namespace
questions.why: The greedy report pod asks for one hundred CPUs. No node has that much free, so it stays Pending, and Kubernetes writes a FailedScheduling Warning event.
explanations: Correct. In Mattermost this alert is orange: it's waiting, not crashing.
An image typo gives ImagePullBackOff, after the pod was scheduled.
A crashing app gives CrashLoopBackOff; this pod never started.
Pod scheduling has nothing to do with n8n's permissions; n8n only reads the result.
questions.takeaway: Pending plus FailedScheduling: check the pod's resource requests against the nodes.

questions.q: The Namespace health report runs every day at 8:00. You've just fixed the cluster and want to see the report now. What do you do?
options: Wait until tomorrow's run at 8:00
Change the schedule to every 30 seconds
Click Execute workflow to run it now
Post the report by hand in Mattermost
questions.why: Execute workflow runs it now. The lesson ran the report before and after fix.sh: three of five pods needed attention, then all two pods were healthy.
explanations: That works, but there is no need to wait to check it.
That would post a full report every 30 seconds: a flood, and the alert workflow already covers fast checks.
Correct. Run it by hand, check the table, and the schedule keeps working for tomorrow.
The point is to see what the workflow builds from the cluster, not to type it yourself.
questions.takeaway: Test a scheduled workflow with Execute workflow instead of waiting for its schedule.

questions.q: On minikube, the alert workflow fails with ECONNREFUSED right after n8n was recreated. What do you do?
options: Disable certificate checks
Give n8n's token cluster-admin rights
Set K8S_API_URL to https://127.0.0.1:8443
Run connect-cluster.sh once more
questions.why: When n8n is recreated it leaves minikube's network. connect-cluster.sh reconnects it, and renews the token.
explanations: Certificate checks protect you from talking to the wrong server; they are not why the connection is refused.
A connection that is refused never gets as far as checking permissions, and cluster-admin would break least privilege.
Inside the n8n container, 127.0.0.1 is n8n itself; that is why the script uses the cluster's internal address.
Correct. It puts n8n back on minikube's network.
questions.takeaway: A recreated container loses extra networks it was connected to: reconnect it.

questions.q: n8n's calls to the cluster fail with a self-signed certificate error. What is the right fix?
options: Turn certificate checks off in the HTTP node
Fix the missing CA file (cluster/ca.crt)
Call the Kubernetes API over plain HTTP
Give n8n's token more permissions in demo
questions.why: n8n checks it is talking to the real cluster with the cluster's certificate authority. The error means the CA file is missing: fix the file, never switch certificate checks off.
explanations: That would let n8n send its token to any server that answers.
Correct. connect-cluster.sh saves the cluster's certificate authority in cluster/ca.crt for n8n.
Plain HTTP would send the token unprotected, and the API serves HTTPS.
Permissions come after the connection; this is a trust problem, not an access problem.
questions.takeaway: Trust the cluster's CA; never disable certificate checks.

questions.q: Right after a fresh start, the workflow alerts about pods that no longer exist. Which part of the workflow prevents this, and why is it needed?
options: One item per event, which splits the list
New problems only, which remembers earlier runs
The filter on events from the last 2 minutes
The Schedule trigger, which waits 30 seconds
questions.why: Kubernetes keeps events for about an hour, so a fresh start would see old warnings. The filter only takes events updated in the last two minutes.
explanations: Splitting turns the list into one item per event; it keeps old events too.
After a fresh start, New problems only has no memory yet: every old pod name looks new.
Correct. Old events about pods that are already gone are dropped.
The trigger only decides when to check, not which events count.
questions.takeaway: Events outlive pods: only act on recent ones.

questions.q: Your team wants the same alerts for a cluster on Amazon EKS. What changes?
options: Same connect-cluster.sh; workflows unchanged
Both workflows must be rewritten for the EKS API
n8n given cluster-admin rights on EKS
A push watcher replaces the polling workflow
questions.why: Nothing here is specific to minikube. connect-cluster.sh uses your cluster's own address and certificate authority and skips the minikube network step; the workflows stay the same. Delete the cluster when you finish.
explanations: Correct. Point kubectl at the cluster (aws eks update-kubeconfig) and run the same script; az aks get-credentials does the same for AKS.
The workflows only use the standard Kubernetes API, which EKS serves as well.
The same read-only Role works on any cluster.
Polling works the same way on EKS; n8n talks to the cluster's public API endpoint or runs in the same network.
questions.takeaway: Plain Kubernetes API + any kubectl context = the same workflows on minikube, EKS or AKS.
